A regular hexagon with side length 4 is subdivided into a lattice of 96 equilateral triangles of side length 1. Let $S$ be the set of all vertices of this lattice. Compute the number of nondegenerate triangles with vertices in $S$ that contain the center of the hexagon strictly in their interior.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(O\) be the center of the hexagon. We will count triangles whose vertices are lattice points other than \(O\), since a triangle that strictly contains \(O\) cannot have \(O\) as a vertex.

Place the triangular lattice in axial coordinates with basis vectors
\[
e_1=(1,0),\qquad e_2=\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right).
\]
The hexagon of side length \(4\) is
\[
\{(i,j)\in \mathbb Z^2:\ |i|\le 4,\ |j|\le 4,\ |i+j|\le 4\}.
\]
It has \(61\) lattice vertices, including the center \(O\), so there are \(60\) nonzero lattice points.

A triangle \(ABC\) contains \(O\) strictly in its interior iff the three rays \(OA,OB,OC\) are not contained in any closed half-plane through \(O\). Equivalently, in their circular order, every angular gap is strictly less than \(180^\circ\). In particular, no two vertices may lie on the same ray or on opposite rays.

Now group the \(60\) nonzero points by the ray from \(O\) on which they lie. In one \(60^\circ\) sector, the primitive directions, in angular order, are
\[
(1,0),\ (3,1),\ (2,1),\ (1,1),\ (1,2),\ (1,3).
\]
Their numbers of lattice points on the ray inside the hexagon are
\[
4,\ 1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 1,\ 1.
\]
By rotational symmetry, over all six sectors the ray weights are:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{weight } w & \text{number of rays} & \text{total points} \\
\hline
4 & 6 & 24\\
2 & 6 & 12\\
1 & 24 & 24
\end{array}
\]
Thus there are \(36\) rays, containing a total of \(60\) nonzero points.

First count all triples of points lying on three distinct rays. From the \(60\) nonzero points,
\[
\binom{60}{3}=34220
\]
triples are possible. Subtract triples with at least two points on the same ray:

- For a ray of weight \(4\): \(\binom42(60-4)+\binom43=6\cdot56+4=340\), and there are \(6\) such rays.
- For a ray of weight \(2\): \(\binom22(60-2)=58\), and there are \(6\) such rays.

So the number of triples on three distinct rays is
\[
34220-6\cdot340-6\cdot58
=34220-2040-348
=31832.
\]

Now subtract the triples that do not strictly contain \(O\).

### 1. Triples contained in an open semicircle

For a ray with \(w\) points, the open \(180^\circ\) arc in one direction from it contains exactly half of the points not on the line through that ray. The line through the ray contains that ray and its opposite, each with \(w\) points, so the open arc has
\[
N=\frac{60-2w}{2}=30-w
\]
points.

Let
\[
\mathcal Q=\sum_{\text{rays}} w^2=6\cdot16+6\cdot4+24\cdot1=144.
\]
By central symmetry, the sum of squares of ray weights in the open arc is
\[
Q=\frac{\mathcal Q-2w^2}{2}=72-w^2.
\]
The number of ways to choose two points on distinct rays in that open arc is
\[
\frac{N^2-Q}{2}.
\]
Multiplying by the \(w\) choices for the point on the starting ray, the contribution for a ray of weight \(w\) is
\[
w\cdot \frac{(30-w)^2-(72-w^2)}2.
\]
Evaluate by weight:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
w & \text{contribution per ray} & \text{number of rays} \\
\hline
4 & 4\cdot\frac{26^2-56}{2}=1240 & 6\\
2 & 2\cdot\frac{28^2-68}{2}=716 & 6\\
1 & 1\cdot\frac{29^2-71}{2}=385 & 24
\end{array}
\]
Thus the number of triples contained in an open semicircle is
\[
6\cdot1240+6\cdot716+24\cdot385
=7440+4296+9240
=20976.
\]

### 2. Triples containing an opposite pair of rays

If a triple contains an opposite pair of rays, then \(O\) lies on a side, so it is not strictly interior.

For an opposite pair of rays each of weight \(w\), there are \(w^2\) choices for the two vertices on those rays, and \(60-2w\) choices for the third vertex on another ray.

There are \(3\) opposite pairs of weight \(4\), \(3\) of weight \(2\), and \(12\) of weight \(1\). Therefore the number of such bad triples is
\[
3\cdot4^2(60-8)+3\cdot2^2(60-4)+12\cdot1^2(60-2)
\]
\[
=3\cdot16\cdot52+3\cdot4\cdot56+12\cdot1\cdot58
=2496+672+696
=3864.
\]

Subtracting both bad types from the distinct-ray triples gives
\[
31832-20976-3864=6992.
\]

Thus the number of nondegenerate triangles with vertices in \(S\) that contain the center strictly in their interior is

\[
\boxed{6992}
\]
